newsitem.title: UK: European bonds take a pounding, led lower by U.S..
newsitem.headline: European bonds take a pounding, led lower by U.S..

text.p: European bond futures skidded again on Wednesday, led lower by a frail U.S. Treasury market and technical year-end selling.
Analysts said there were few fundamental factors at play but the market was anxious, especially after recent turbulence.
"The market's very very nervous," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London.
"Once it does break some key levels, it just exaggerates itself and everyone jumps on the bandwagon."
March Bund futures tumbled to a 99.99 low in the morning session on LIFFE and by 1120 GMT were down 0.66 at 100.14.
It was a similar story elsewhere, with March British gilts off 20/32 at 109-17 and the March French notionnel down 0.50 at 128.30 and March Italian BTP futures 0.72 lower at 127.77.

"Technically these markets are starting to look much more negative, said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "My gut reaction is people are taking profits into the year-end after a good year."
Beauchamp said the break of the 100.35 level triggered additional selling in the German market.
"As soon as we got below that real cash sellers started coming out of Germany. That's put quite a bit of pressure on the market. It's trying to find some support around the par level," he said.
U.S. Treasuries have been hurt by worries that investors, particularly Japanese players, will cash in before the year-end after a relatively bullish period in the past couple of months.

Japanese investors had been notable earlier in the year for a yen-based strategy where they borrowed in yen at extremely low interest rates, switched into dollars and then bought U.S. Treasuries which were yielding more than domestic Japanese debt.
The trade had extra appeal in that it took advantage of a rising dollar/yen rate as well, analysts said.
The U.S. long bond was quoted in London at 99-17, to yield 6.53 percent, down from 99-24 at the close in Tokyo and 100-04 in New York on Tuesday.
"There's been a bit of a beating in the U.S. market," McDevitt said. "There hasn't been any new information in Europe. They're taking their lead from the U.S."
